newsitem.title: CHINA: Further China rate cut seen on dipping prices.
newsitem.headline: Further China rate cut seen on dipping prices.

text.p: Slowing exports, weak consumer demand and bumper harvests have put China on track for lower-than-expected inflation of about six percent in 1996, making a further interest rate cut possible, economists said on Friday.

China's retail price inflation rose a year-on-year 6.6 percent in the first nine months, while inflation for September rose five percent compared with the year-ago month, its lowest level in some three years, the State Statistical Bureau said.
"Inflation in the last quarter is expected to be lower than that in the first nine months," Chen Dezun, director of the Price Research Institute under the State Planning Commission said.
"The trend should lead to an annual inflation rate of about six percent for 1996," he said in a telephone interview.
China has set a target of 10 percent retail price inflation for 1996, down from 14.8 percent in 1995. China's retail price inflation hit a Communist-era high of 21.7 percent in 1994.
"The drop in inflation is mainly because of a slowdown in the growth of exports this year," Chen said.
Sluggish exports had slashed consumer demand while goods that had failed to find overseas buyers had entered the domestic market where supply already outstripped consumption, he said.
China's exports totalled $90.612 billion in the first eight months, down 4.2 percent from the same period in 1995, customs figures showed. The surplus was $4.997 billion.
China's three-year-old austerity programme designed to curb inflation had hit the domestic consumer market, he said.
A bumper grain harvest in 1995 and again this summer had played an important role in bringing down inflation, said economist Yang Fan of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.
China has said grain production would reach 475 million tonnes this year, up from a record 466 million tonnes in 1995.
"Falling prices will allow China to further reduce interest rates," Elizabeth Cheng, head of China research at Wardley James Capel (Far East) said by telephone from Hong Kong.
China has cut interest rates twice this year to boost the economy as inflation has slowed more quickly than expected.
Yang said he expected a further easing in monetary policy.
"A further rate cut is likely because inflation is falling rather rapidly," he said. He expected the central bank to trim interest rates by an average of one percentage point in 1997.

However, long-term pressure on China's prices still existed, warned Chen of the State Planning Commission. Growth of China's broad M2 money supply remained high and could push up buying power in the future.
China's broad M2 money supply rose by 27.5 percent in January to August compared with a year ago, official media quoted the central bank as saying. China's M2 growth target is 25 percent for 1996.
Inflation could resurge if the government tried to stimulate investment and the consumer markets by loosening its tight monetary policy, he warned.
Gross domestic product was expected to grow by about 10 percent in 1996, Chen said.

Officials have set a target of about nine percent to try to cool an economy that has shown signs of overheating in the past three years and Western economists said they expected growth to reach that goal.
